anchors.title: Lovelace's objection
anchors.story: In her notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, Ada Lovelace argued the machine had no power to originate anything — it could only do what a person already knew how to order it to do. The question of whether a machine can truly originate something new, rather than just follow instructions, is still argued about today.

source.label: Ada Lovelace, "Notes" (Note G, 1843), on Menabrea's sketch of the Analytical Engine — primary source

anchors.title: Turing's machine question
anchors.story: Alan Turing's 1936 paper gave a precise mathematical model of computation. In 1950 he shifted the public question from abstract definitions of thinking to an operational test: could a machine's behavior in conversation be indistinguishable from a person's?

source.label: Turing, "On Computable Numbers" (1936); "Computing Machinery and Intelligence", Mind (1950)

anchors.title: Poland breaks Enigma first
anchors.story: Polish Cipher Bureau mathematicians Marian Rejewski, Jerzy Różycki, and Henryk Zygalski reverse-engineered the German Enigma machine from theory alone, years before the Second World War. In July 1939 they handed their reconstructed machine and decryption methods to French and British intelligence — directly seeding the more famous Bletchley Park codebreaking effort that followed.

source.label: IEEE Milestones: First Breaking of the Enigma Code by the Team of Polish Cipher Bureau, 1932-1939

anchors.title: McCulloch–Pitts artificial neuron
anchors.story: Neurophysiologist Warren McCulloch and logician Walter Pitts published the first mathematical model treating a brain neuron as a simple logic gate: it fires or doesn't, based on weighted inputs crossing a threshold. This is the direct mathematical ancestor of every artificial neural network built since.

source.label: McCulloch, W. & Pitts, W. (1943), "A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity," Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics

anchors.title: Dartmouth names artificial intelligence
anchors.story: A summer research proposal at Dartmouth College gathered researchers around the claim that aspects of learning and intelligence could be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate them. The meeting gave the new research field a durable name and institutional center.

source.label: "A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence" (1955) — primary source

anchors.title: Wittgenstein: meaning as use
anchors.story: In the Tractatus (1921), the young Wittgenstein treated language as a picture of logical facts. By the posthumous Philosophical Investigations (1953), he argued instead that meaning comes from how a word is used within a shared context, not from a fixed picture it represents — a lens later writers apply to how language models derive meaning from patterns of use.

anchors.title: Backpropagation spreads
anchors.story: David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams published a widely read demonstration of backpropagation — an algorithm for training multi-layer neural networks by pushing errors backward through the network to adjust each connection. This is a popularization, not the idea's origin, but it made the technique legible and usable across the field.

source.label: Rumelhart, D., Hinton, G. & Williams, R. (1986), "Learning representations by back-propagating errors," Nature

anchors.title: The Transformer arrives
anchors.story: Ashish Vaswani and seven co-authors at Google published "Attention Is All You Need," introducing the Transformer architecture — built entirely around an attention mechanism rather than the recurrent networks that came before. Every major large language model since descends from this architecture.

source.label: Vaswani et al. (2017), "Attention Is All You Need," arXiv

anchors.title: The hidden labor behind AI
anchors.story: Low-paid workers, including annotators in Kenya employed by outsourcing firms, label and review the data and model outputs that make deployed AI systems work — including reviewing disturbing content to help train safety filters. Exact conditions and figures are contested in reporting; the phenomenon itself is well-documented.

source.label: Billy Perrigo, "OpenAI Used Kenyan Workers on Less Than $2 Per Hour," TIME (2023)
